u:cp-strategy-0-read-the-whole-set-first.title: Read the whole set first
u:cp-strategy-0-read-the-whole-set-first.summary: Skim every problem before coding; the easiest isn't always A.

blocks.text: At the start, quickly read **all** problems and note which look easiest. Contest problems aren't strictly ordered by difficulty for everyone — a later problem may be your fastest solve.
Solve in order of *your* confidence and speed, not the label order.

options: The easiest for you may not be problem A
mcqs.explain: Difficulty is subjective; find your quick wins.

mcqs.q: You should attempt problems in order of:
mcqs.explain: Prioritise what you can solve fastest.

mcqs.q: Reading the full set costs a few minutes but:
mcqs.explain: It surfaces the best-value problems early.

u:cp-strategy-1-time-management-and-prob.title: Time management & problem order
u:cp-strategy-1-time-management-and-prob.summary: Budget time per problem; don't sink the whole contest into one.

blocks.text: Allocate time and **move on** when stuck. Sinking 45 minutes into one hard problem often costs two easier solves. Come back with fresh eyes if time remains.
A rough rule: if you have no idea after ~10-15 min, switch problems.

mcqs.q: When you're badly stuck on a problem you should:
options: Move to another and return later
Keep grinding it to the end
mcqs.explain: Switching preserves time for solvable problems.

mcqs.q: Over-investing in one hard problem risks:
mcqs.explain: Time is the scarce resource.

mcqs.q: Coming back to a problem later helps because:
mcqs.explain: A break often unblocks the insight.

u:cp-strategy-2-reading-constraints-to-p.title: Reading constraints to pick complexity
u:cp-strategy-2-reading-constraints-to-p.summary: Constraints tell you the target time complexity before you code.

blocks.text: The **constraints** (e.g. n ≤ 10^5) hint at the intended complexity. Aim for roughly ≤ 10^8 operations per second.
Read n first — it eliminates whole categories of approaches instantly.

mcqs.q: If n ≤ 10^5, an O(n^2) solution will likely:
mcqs.explain: 10^10 ops is far beyond the ~10^8/sec budget.

mcqs.q: n up to ~20 often hints at:
mcqs.explain: Small n allows exponential methods.
They bound the acceptable running time.

u:cp-strategy-3-penalty-and-scoring-syst.title: Penalty & scoring systems
u:cp-strategy-3-penalty-and-scoring-syst.summary: ICPC-style penalises wrong submissions and time; know your contest's rules.

blocks.text: Formats differ. **ICPC-style** ranks by problems solved, breaking ties by total time + a penalty per wrong submission. **IOI/points-style** gives partial credit per subtask. Codeforces uses a decaying score with penalties for wrong attempts.
Under penalty systems, don't spam submissions — test locally first; each wrong try costs time/points.

mcqs.q: In ICPC-style scoring, wrong submissions add:
mcqs.explain: Each wrong attempt adds penalty minutes.
Test locally to avoid penalties.
Subtasks give partial scores.

u:cp-strategy-4-when-to-skip-or-switch.title: When to skip or switch
u:cp-strategy-4-when-to-skip-or-switch.summary: Recognise sunk cost; a stuck problem now may be an easy solve later.

blocks.text: Guard against **sunk-cost** thinking. The time already spent doesn't justify more if you're not converging. Note your idea, switch, and return if time allows.
Write down where you're stuck before switching — restarting is faster later.

mcqs.explain: Past time shouldn't dictate future time.
Notes speed up your return.

mcqs.q: The decision to switch depends on:
options: Whether you're converging on a solution
mcqs.explain: Progress, not the label, guides switching.

u:cp-strategy-5-upsolving-after-the-cont.title: Upsolving after the contest
u:cp-strategy-5-upsolving-after-the-cont.summary: Solve the problems you couldn't during the contest — that's where growth happens.

blocks.text: **Upsolving** — solving problems you missed after the contest ends — is the single biggest driver of improvement. Read the editorial only after a real attempt, then re-implement from scratch.
Rating comes from contests; skill comes from upsolving.

options: Solving missed problems after the contest
mcqs.explain: You finish the problems you couldn't in time.
Struggle first, then learn from the editorial.
It's the core learning loop.

u:cp-complexity-0-big-o-refresher.title: Big-O refresher
u:cp-complexity-0-big-o-refresher.summary: Big-O describes how running time grows with input size.

blocks.text: **Big-O** captures the dominant growth term as n grows, ignoring constants. Common orders (fastest to slowest): O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n) < O(n!).
You compare algorithms by their Big-O for large n; constants matter only when orders tie.

mcqs.explain: Factorial dominates all the others.
It focuses on asymptotic growth.
Halving the range each step is logarithmic.

u:cp-complexity-1-operations-budget-10-8.title: Operations budget (~10^8/sec)
u:cp-complexity-1-operations-budget-10-8.summary: A rough rule: ~10^8 simple operations run in about a second.

blocks.text: A useful mental model: modern judges handle roughly **10^8 simple operations per second**. Estimate your solution's op count from its complexity and the max n to predict TLE before submitting.
This is a rough guide — constant factors, I/O, and language (Python is slower) shift it a lot.

mcqs.q: A rough per-second op budget is:
mcqs.explain: About 100 million simple ops per second.

mcqs.q: For n=10^6, an O(n^2) solution does ~10^12 ops, which:
mcqs.explain: 10^12 far exceeds the ~10^8/sec budget.
I/O, constants, and language all matter.

u:cp-complexity-2-constraints-to-complex.title: Constraints to complexity table
u:cp-complexity-2-constraints-to-complex.summary: Map the max n to the complexity you can afford.

blocks.text: Memorise the constraint→complexity mapping so you pick an approach instantly (see the strategy note). n ≤ 10^5 → O(n log n); n ≤ 5000 → O(n^2); n ≤ 20 → O(2^n).
If your first idea's complexity is too slow for the constraints, don't code it — find a better one first.

mcqs.explain: ~25M ops fits the budget.
Only near-linear passes at that size.
Match the approach to constraints up front.

u:cp-complexity-3-constant-factors-and-i.title: Constant factors & I/O speed
u:cp-complexity-3-constant-factors-and-i.summary: Two same-Big-O solutions can differ 10x; slow I/O alone can TLE.

blocks.text: Big-O ties are broken by **constant factors**: cache-friendly arrays beat pointer-chasing; avoiding needless allocations helps. **Slow input reading** (e.g. unbuffered cin, Scanner, input()) can cause TLE by itself at 10^6 lines.
Use fast I/O for large inputs: sync_with_stdio(false) in C++, BufferedReader in Java, sys.stdin in Python.

mcqs.q: Two O(n) solutions can still differ by:
mcqs.explain: Constants and memory layout matter when orders tie.
Unbuffered I/O is a common hidden bottleneck.
Untying and unsyncing streams speeds cin/cout.

u:cp-math-0-modular-arithmetic.title: Modular arithmetic
u:cp-math-0-modular-arithmetic.summary: Take results mod a prime (often 10^9+7) to keep numbers in range.

blocks.text: Answers that grow huge are asked **modulo** a large prime (commonly 1e9+7). Addition and multiplication distribute over mod: (a+b)%m, (a*b)%m. Take mod after every operation to avoid overflow.
Subtraction can go negative: use ((a-b)%m + m) % m. Division needs a modular inverse, not plain /.

mcqs.explain: 10^9+7 is a standard large prime.
Apply mod after each multiply.
Add m before the final mod.

u:cp-math-1-modular-exponentiation-fast-.title: Modular exponentiation (fast power)
u:cp-math-1-modular-exponentiation-fast-.summary: Compute a^b mod m in O(log b) by squaring.

blocks.text: **Fast exponentiation** computes a^b in O(log b) by repeatedly squaring the base and multiplying when the current bit of b is 1.

mcqs.explain: Each step halves the exponent.

options: Squaring the base and using b's bits
mcqs.explain: Binary exponentiation squares and multiplies.
Naive a^b would be far too slow/overflow.

u:cp-math-2-modular-inverse.title: Modular inverse
u:cp-math-2-modular-inverse.summary: Divide under a prime mod via Fermat: a^(m-2) mod m.

blocks.text: Under a **prime** modulus m, division a/b becomes a * b^(m-2) mod m by **Fermat's little theorem** — b^(m-2) is the modular inverse of b. Compute it with fast power.
Modular inverse only works this way when m is prime and b is not a multiple of m.

mcqs.q: Under prime m, the inverse of b is:
mcqs.explain: Fermat's little theorem gives b^(m-2).

mcqs.q: You need a modular inverse to:
mcqs.explain: Plain division doesn't work modulo m.
The theorem needs m prime.

u:cp-math-3-gcd-lcm-and-euclid.title: GCD/LCM & Euclid
u:cp-math-3-gcd-lcm-and-euclid.summary: Euclid's algorithm finds gcd fast; lcm = a/gcd*b.

blocks.text: **Euclid's algorithm**: gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a%b), terminating when b=0. **LCM** = a / gcd(a,b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow).
int gcd(int a,int b){ return b? gcd(b, a%b) : a; }

mcqs.explain: Repeated remainder shrinks the pair fast.
Divide by gcd first to avoid overflow.
It's logarithmic in the smaller value.

u:cp-math-4-sieve-of-eratosthenes.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes
u:cp-math-4-sieve-of-eratosthenes.summary: Precompute all primes up to n in O(n log log n).

blocks.text: The **sieve** marks multiples of each prime as composite, leaving primes up to n in about O(n log log n). Great when you need many primality checks or all primes in a range.

mcqs.explain: It precomputes primality for 2..n.
Near-linear for the whole range.

mcqs.q: Inner marking starts at i*i because:
mcqs.explain: Multiples below i*i were struck by smaller primes.

u:cp-math-5-prime-factorization.title: Prime factorization
u:cp-math-5-prime-factorization.summary: Trial-divide up to sqrt(n); a sieve of smallest-prime-factors speeds many factorizations.

blocks.text: Factor n by dividing out primes up to **sqrt(n)**; any remainder > 1 is a prime factor. For many queries, precompute the **smallest prime factor** with a sieve to factor in O(log n).
Only test divisors up to sqrt(n) — a factor larger than sqrt(n) pairs with one smaller.

mcqs.q: Trial-division factorization tests divisors up to:
mcqs.explain: Beyond sqrt(n), factors pair with smaller ones.
SPF gives O(log n) factorization per query.

mcqs.q: After dividing out all primes ≤ sqrt(n), a remainder > 1 is:
mcqs.explain: The leftover must itself be prime.

u:cp-math-6-combinatorics-ncr-with-mod.title: Combinatorics (nCr) with mod
u:cp-math-6-combinatorics-ncr-with-mod.summary: Precompute factorials and inverse factorials for O(1) nCr mod p.

blocks.text: To compute **nCr mod p** quickly, precompute factorials fact[] and inverse factorials. Then nCr = fact[n] * invfact[r] % p * invfact[n-r] % p.
Precompute inverse factorials from invfact[n] downward using invfact[i-1] = invfact[i]*i % p.

mcqs.q: nCr mod p is computed with:
mcqs.explain: Precomputed factorials give O(1) queries.

mcqs.q: The inverse factorial is needed because:
options: Division under mod needs an inverse
mcqs.explain: nCr divides by r! and (n-r)!.

mcqs.q: After precomputation, each nCr query is:
mcqs.explain: It's three array lookups and multiplies.

u:cp-math-7-overflow-and-big-numbers.title: Overflow & big numbers
u:cp-math-7-overflow-and-big-numbers.summary: int overflows near 2*10^9; use 64-bit and mod early.

blocks.text: A 32-bit int holds up to ~2.1×10^9. Multiplying two large ints overflows silently. Use **64-bit** (long long / long) and apply **mod** during multiplication to stay in range.
a*b where a,b ~10^9 overflows 32-bit even if the modded answer is small — cast/mod before it overflows.

mcqs.explain: Signed 32-bit maxes around 2^31-1.

mcqs.q: To multiply two ~10^9 numbers safely use:
mcqs.explain: Use long long and mod during the product.
It wraps/UB without warning — a classic bug.

u:cp-techniques-0-greedy-method.title: Greedy method
u:cp-techniques-0-greedy-method.summary: Make the locally-best choice; prove it yields a global optimum.

blocks.text: A **greedy** algorithm builds a solution by always taking the locally optimal choice. It's fast but only correct when the problem has the greedy-choice property — otherwise it fails on some case.
Always sanity-check greed with a counterexample or an exchange argument; many greedy 'solutions' are wrong.

mcqs.explain: Greedy commits to the local optimum.

options: The problem has the greedy-choice property
mcqs.explain: It needs a proof/exchange argument.

mcqs.q: A safe habit before trusting greedy is:
mcqs.explain: Test the greedy choice for validity.

u:cp-techniques-1-sorting-based-greedy.title: Sorting-based greedy
u:cp-techniques-1-sorting-based-greedy.summary: Sorting first often unlocks a simple greedy (intervals, deadlines).

blocks.text: Many greedy problems become clear after **sorting** — e.g. activity selection sorts by end time; job scheduling sorts by deadline/profit. The sort sets up the order in which greedy choices are safe.
When a greedy idea feels close but flaky, try a different sort key.

mcqs.q: Activity selection (max non-overlapping intervals) sorts by:
mcqs.explain: Earliest finishing frees the most room.
The right order makes the greedy valid.

mcqs.q: If a greedy is flaky, a good tweak is:
mcqs.explain: The sort criterion is often the fix.

u:cp-techniques-2-two-pointers.title: Two pointers
u:cp-techniques-2-two-pointers.summary: Move two indices over sorted/linear data to hit O(n) instead of O(n^2).

blocks.text: The **two-pointer** technique uses two indices moving over an array (often sorted) to replace nested loops. Classic uses: pair with target sum, merging, removing duplicates.
Each pointer moves monotonically, so total work is O(n) even though it looks like two loops.

mcqs.q: Two pointers typically reduce O(n^2) to:
mcqs.explain: Both pointers sweep once.

options: Pair summing to a target in a sorted array
mcqs.explain: Move pointers inward based on the sum.

mcqs.q: Two pointers are efficient because each index:
mcqs.explain: No backtracking keeps it linear.

u:cp-techniques-3-sliding-window.title: Sliding window
u:cp-techniques-3-sliding-window.summary: A moving window over a subarray computes range answers in O(n).

blocks.text: A **sliding window** maintains a contiguous range [l, r], expanding r and shrinking l to satisfy a condition (max sum of size k, longest substring without repeats). Update the running answer incrementally instead of recomputing.
Fixed-size windows slide by adding the new element and removing the old; variable windows shrink l while a condition is violated.

mcqs.q: A sliding window computes subarray answers in:
mcqs.explain: Each element enters and leaves once.

mcqs.q: A variable-size window shrinks l when:
mcqs.explain: Shrink until the window is valid again.
It updates the answer incrementally.

u:cp-techniques-4-prefix-sums.title: Prefix sums
u:cp-techniques-4-prefix-sums.summary: Precompute cumulative sums for O(1) range-sum queries.

blocks.text: A **prefix-sum** array pre[i] = a[0]+…+a[i-1] lets you answer any range sum a[l..r] as pre[r+1]-pre[l] in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing.

mcqs.q: A range sum with prefix sums is:
mcqs.explain: One subtraction per query.
Difference of prefix boundaries.

mcqs.q: Prefix sums help most when there are:
mcqs.explain: They amortise repeated range queries.

u:cp-techniques-5-difference-arrays.title: Difference arrays
u:cp-techniques-5-difference-arrays.summary: Apply many range updates in O(1) each, then one pass to finalise.

blocks.text: A **difference array** applies range updates cheaply: to add v to [l, r], do diff[l]+=v and diff[r+1]-=v. A single prefix-sum pass at the end reconstructs the final array — O(1) per update, O(n) to finalise.
It's the inverse of prefix sums — great for 'add v to a range' done many times.

mcqs.q: A difference array makes each range update:
mcqs.explain: Two edits per update, finalised later.

mcqs.q: To add v to [l,r] you set:
mcqs.explain: The two edits bound the range.
Prefix-summing the diff array finalises it.

u:cp-techniques-6-binary-search-on-answe.title: Binary search on answer
u:cp-techniques-6-binary-search-on-answe.summary: When feasibility is monotonic in x, binary search the smallest/largest valid x.

blocks.text: If 'can we achieve x?' is **monotonic** (true beyond some threshold, false before), binary search the boundary. Common in min-max problems ('minimize the maximum…'). Each step checks feasibility in O(n).
Look for the phrase 'minimize the maximum' or 'maximum minimum' — a strong signal for binary search on the answer.

mcqs.q: Binary search on the answer needs the check to be:
mcqs.explain: Feasibility must flip once as x grows.
Min-max phrasing signals BS on the answer.
log(range) checks, each O(n).

u:cp-techniques-7-bit-manipulation-trick.title: Bit manipulation tricks
u:cp-techniques-7-bit-manipulation-trick.summary: Bitwise ops enable subsets, parity, and fast set operations.

items: `x & (x-1)` clears the lowest set bit; `x & -x` isolates it.
Iterate all subsets of an n-bit mask for bitmask DP.

blocks.text: Bitmasks represent small sets (n ≤ ~20) compactly — the basis of subset DP.

mcqs.explain: It removes the least significant 1.

mcqs.q: Bitmasks are practical for sets of size up to about:
mcqs.explain: 2^20 ~ 10^6 subsets is the practical ceiling.

mcqs.q: Testing whether bit k is set uses:
mcqs.explain: AND with the k-th bit mask.

u:cp-techniques-8-recursion-and-backtrac.title: Recursion & backtracking
u:cp-techniques-8-recursion-and-backtrac.summary: Explore choices recursively, undoing them to try alternatives.

blocks.text: **Backtracking** builds candidates incrementally and abandons ('backtracks') a partial solution once it can't lead to a valid one (permutations, N-queens, subsets). Prune early to cut the search space.
The pattern: choose → recurse → undo. Pruning invalid branches is what makes it feasible.

mcqs.q: Backtracking abandons a partial solution when:
options: It can't lead to a valid one
mcqs.explain: Prune dead branches early.
Make a choice, recurse, then revert it.
Early cutoffs make exponential search tractable.

u:cp-techniques-9-meet-in-the-middle.title: Meet in the middle
u:cp-techniques-9-meet-in-the-middle.summary: Split the search space in two halves to turn 2^n into ~2^(n/2).

blocks.text: **Meet in the middle** splits a size-n exponential search into two halves, enumerates each (2^(n/2)), and combines them (often by sorting + binary search). It makes n up to ~40 feasible where full 2^n wouldn't be.
Use it for subset-sum-style problems with n around 30-40.

mcqs.q: Meet in the middle reduces 2^n to about:
mcqs.explain: Two halves of 2^(n/2) combine.
Full 2^n is too slow past ~25-30.

mcqs.q: The two halves are combined by:
mcqs.explain: Match sums across halves efficiently.

u:cp-ds-0-stack-queue-deque-uses.title: Stack, queue, deque uses
u:cp-ds-0-stack-queue-deque-uses.summary: LIFO/FIFO/double-ended structures power many linear-time tricks.

blocks.text: A **stack** (LIFO) underpins monotonic-stack tricks (next greater element, largest rectangle). A **queue** (FIFO) drives BFS. A **deque** supports both ends — used in sliding-window maximum.
A monotonic stack/deque answers 'nearest greater/smaller' and window extremes in O(n).

mcqs.explain: FIFO order explores level by level.

mcqs.q: Sliding-window maximum in O(n) uses a:
mcqs.explain: A monotonic deque tracks candidates.
It processes each element once in O(n).

u:cp-ds-1-hash-maps-and-frequency.title: Hash maps & frequency
u:cp-ds-1-hash-maps-and-frequency.summary: O(1) average lookup for counting, grouping, and seen-checks.

blocks.text: **Hash maps** give average O(1) insert/lookup — ideal for frequency counts, grouping by key, and 'have I seen this?' checks. In C++ prefer unordered_map (watch anti-hash tests) or a sorted map for guarantees.
unordered_map can be attacked to O(n) per op with crafted keys; add a random salt or use a tree map if TLE hits.

mcqs.explain: Average constant time.
Counting/grouping is their sweet spot.
Anti-hash inputs cause worst-case chains.

u:cp-ds-2-priority-queue-heap.title: Priority queue / heap
u:cp-ds-2-priority-queue-heap.summary: Always pop the min/max in O(log n) — powers Dijkstra and scheduling.

blocks.text: A **heap / priority queue** gives the smallest (or largest) element in O(log n) per push/pop. It powers Dijkstra, k-largest problems, and event scheduling.
Building a heap from n items is O(n); each subsequent pop/push is O(log n).

mcqs.explain: Sift up/down is logarithmic.
It repeatedly extracts the min-distance node.

mcqs.q: Building a heap from n items is:
mcqs.explain: Heapify is linear.

u:cp-ds-3-union-find-dsu.title: Union-Find (DSU)
u:cp-ds-3-union-find-dsu.summary: Near-O(1) union/find with path compression + union by rank.

blocks.text: **Disjoint Set Union** tracks connected components with `find` (which set?) and `union` (merge). With **path compression** and **union by rank/size** each op is near O(1) (inverse-Ackermann).

int find(int x){ return p[x]==x? x : p[x]=find(p[x]); }
void uni(int a,int b){ p[find(a)]=find(b); }

mcqs.explain: It answers connectivity/merge queries.

mcqs.q: Path compression + union by rank make ops:
mcqs.explain: Amortised inverse-Ackermann.
It merges components while building an MST.

u:cp-ds-4-segment-tree-intro.title: Segment tree (intro)
u:cp-ds-4-segment-tree-intro.summary: Range queries + point/range updates in O(log n).

blocks.text: A **segment tree** supports range queries (sum/min/max) and updates in O(log n) over an array. Each node covers a range; queries combine O(log n) node results. Lazy propagation adds efficient range updates.
Reach for it when you need both updates and range queries; prefix sums only handle static range queries.

mcqs.explain: Both are logarithmic.

mcqs.q: Compared to prefix sums, a segment tree also supports:
mcqs.explain: Prefix sums can't handle updates efficiently.
Lazy defers updates to children.

u:cp-ds-5-fenwick-bit-intro.title: Fenwick / BIT (intro)
u:cp-ds-5-fenwick-bit-intro.summary: A compact structure for prefix sums with point updates in O(log n).

blocks.text: A **Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree)** supports prefix sums and point updates in O(log n) with less code and memory than a segment tree — ideal when you only need sum/updates.
Use a BIT for order-statistics and inversion counting; use a segment tree when you need min/max or range updates.

mcqs.q: A Fenwick tree gives prefix sums + point updates in:
mcqs.explain: Both operations are logarithmic.

mcqs.q: Compared to a segment tree, a BIT is:
mcqs.explain: Less code/memory, but sum-focused.
Order statistics/inversions fit BITs well.

u:cp-graphs-0-graph-representation.title: Graph representation
u:cp-graphs-0-graph-representation.summary: Adjacency lists suit sparse graphs; matrices suit dense/small ones.

blocks.text: Store a graph as an **adjacency list** (array of neighbor lists) for sparse graphs — O(V+E) space. Use an **adjacency matrix** only for small/dense graphs (O(V^2)).
Most contest graphs are sparse — default to adjacency lists.

mcqs.explain: Lists use O(V+E) space.
It stores every possible edge slot.
You visit each vertex and edge once.

u:cp-graphs-1-bfs-and-shortest-path-unwe.title: BFS & shortest path (unweighted)
u:cp-graphs-1-bfs-and-shortest-path-unwe.summary: BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs in O(V+E).

blocks.text: **Breadth-first search** explores level by level using a queue, giving the **shortest path in an unweighted graph** (fewest edges) in O(V+E). Track visited to avoid re-processing.
BFS = shortest path when every edge has equal weight. For weights, use Dijkstra.

mcqs.q: BFS gives shortest paths when edges are:
mcqs.explain: Level order = fewest edges.
FIFO gives level-by-level order.
Each vertex/edge processed once.

u:cp-graphs-2-dfs-and-connected-componen.title: DFS & connected components
u:cp-graphs-2-dfs-and-connected-componen.summary: DFS explores deeply; it finds components, cycles, and more.

blocks.text: **Depth-first search** dives along each branch before backtracking (recursion or a stack). It counts **connected components**, detects cycles, and underlies topological sort and bridge/articulation algorithms.
Watch recursion depth on large graphs — deep DFS can stack-overflow; use an explicit stack if needed.

mcqs.explain: Each DFS from an unvisited node = one component.
It goes deep before wide.

mcqs.q: A risk of recursive DFS on big graphs is:
mcqs.explain: Deep recursion can exhaust the stack.

u:cp-graphs-3-dijkstra-weighted-shortest.title: Dijkstra (weighted shortest path)
u:cp-graphs-3-dijkstra-weighted-shortest.summary: Shortest paths with non-negative weights in O(E log V) via a heap.

blocks.text: **Dijkstra's algorithm** finds shortest paths from a source in a graph with **non-negative** edge weights, using a priority queue to always expand the closest unfinished node — O(E log V).
Dijkstra fails with negative edges; use Bellman-Ford there.

mcqs.q: Dijkstra requires edge weights to be:
mcqs.explain: Negative edges break its greedy invariant.

mcqs.q: With a heap, Dijkstra runs in:
mcqs.explain: Each edge triggers a log-V heap op.

mcqs.q: For graphs with negative edges use:
mcqs.explain: Bellman-Ford handles negatives (and detects negative cycles).

u:cp-graphs-4-topological-sort.title: Topological sort
u:cp-graphs-4-topological-sort.summary: Order a DAG so every edge points forward; enables DAG DP.

blocks.text: A **topological sort** linearly orders a **DAG** so every edge u→v has u before v. Compute it via Kahn's algorithm (repeatedly remove zero-indegree nodes) or DFS finish times. It's the basis for dependency resolution and DAG DP.
A topological order exists iff the graph has no cycle — Kahn's also detects cycles.

mcqs.explain: It needs a directed acyclic graph.

mcqs.q: Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes nodes with:
mcqs.explain: Zero-indegree nodes have no unmet prerequisites.

mcqs.q: A topological order fails to exist when the graph:
mcqs.explain: Cycles create circular dependencies.

u:cp-dp-0-dp-fundamentals-states-and-tra.title: DP fundamentals (states & transitions)
u:cp-dp-0-dp-fundamentals-states-and-tra.summary: Define a state, a transition, and base cases; memoize overlapping subproblems.

blocks.text: **Dynamic programming** solves problems with **overlapping subproblems** and **optimal substructure** by defining a **state** (what uniquely describes a subproblem), a **transition** (how states combine), and **base cases**. Memoize (top-down) or tabulate (bottom-up).
Getting the state definition right is 90% of DP — it must capture everything the transition needs.

mcqs.q: DP applies when a problem has:
mcqs.explain: Those two properties enable reuse.

mcqs.q: The hardest, most important DP step is:
mcqs.explain: A correct state makes transitions follow.
It caches subproblem results.

u:cp-dp-1-0-1-knapsack.title: 0/1 Knapsack
u:cp-dp-1-0-1-knapsack.summary: Maximize value within a weight limit; each item taken once.

blocks.text: **0/1 Knapsack**: given items with weights/values and a capacity W, maximize value taking each item at most once. State dp[i][w] = best value using the first i items with capacity w; transition = take or skip item i. O(nW).
dp is over capacity, so it's 'pseudo-polynomial' — feasible only when W is small enough.

mcqs.explain: 0/1 means take-or-leave, once.
n items times W capacities.

mcqs.q: Knapsack DP is called pseudo-polynomial because it depends on:
mcqs.explain: Runtime scales with W's magnitude.

u:cp-dp-2-longest-increasing-subsequence.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
u:cp-dp-2-longest-increasing-subsequence.summary: LIS in O(n log n) with patience/binary search.

blocks.text: **LIS** finds the longest strictly increasing subsequence. The O(n^2) DP is simple; the O(n log n) method keeps an array of smallest tails and binary-searches each element's position.
The 'tails' array length at the end is the LIS length — but the array itself isn't a valid subsequence.

mcqs.explain: Patience sorting + binary search.

mcqs.q: The O(n log n) method maintains:
mcqs.explain: Binary search places each element into tails.

mcqs.q: The tails array's final length equals:
mcqs.explain: Its length is the answer (not the subsequence).

u:cp-dp-3-grid-path-dp.title: Grid / path DP
u:cp-dp-3-grid-path-dp.summary: Count or optimize paths through a grid with dp[i][j] from neighbors.

blocks.text: **Grid DP** computes dp[i][j] from already-solved neighbors (usually top and left) — counting paths, min path sum, or reachability. O(rows×cols).
Handle blocked cells by setting their dp to 0 (paths) or infinity (min-cost).

mcqs.q: Grid path DP fills dp[i][j] from:
mcqs.explain: Transitions come from adjacent subproblems.
Each cell computed once.

mcqs.q: A blocked cell in a path-count DP is set to:
mcqs.explain: No paths pass through it.

u:cp-dp-4-interval-dp.title: Interval DP
u:cp-dp-4-interval-dp.summary: Solve over subranges [l..r], combining across a split point k.

blocks.text: **Interval DP** computes an answer for a range [l, r] by trying every split point k between them (matrix-chain multiplication, optimal BST, burst balloons). Typically O(n^3).
Process intervals by increasing length so smaller ranges are ready when you combine them.

mcqs.explain: It tries each partition of the interval.
n^2 intervals times an n split loop.
Smaller intervals must be solved first.

u:cp-practical-0-fast-i-o.title: Fast I/O
u:cp-practical-0-fast-i-o.summary: Large inputs need buffered/fast reading to avoid TLE.

blocks.text: For inputs with 10^5-10^6 lines, default I/O can TLE. Use **fast I/O**: C++ `ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr);`, Java `BufferedReader`, Python `sys.stdin.readline`.
In C++, mixing fast cin/cout with printf/scanf after unsyncing can misorder output — pick one.

mcqs.q: Fast I/O matters when input has:
mcqs.explain: Large I/O dominates otherwise.
Untie/unsync speeds streams.
sys.stdin.readline is much faster than input().

u:cp-practical-1-common-pitfalls-and-deb.title: Common pitfalls & debugging
u:cp-practical-1-common-pitfalls-and-deb.summary: Overflow, off-by-one, uninitialized state, and edge cases cause most WAs.

items: **Uninitialized / not reset** state between test cases.
**Edge cases**: n=0/1, empty input, all-equal, maximum values.

blocks.text: Between multi-testcase runs, reset all global arrays/counters — leftover state is a classic WA.

mcqs.q: A very common source of wrong answers is:
mcqs.explain: Silent overflow corrupts results.
Leftover globals cause WA.
Boundaries expose most bugs.

u:cp-practical-2-stress-testing.title: Stress testing
u:cp-practical-2-stress-testing.summary: Generate random inputs and compare a brute force vs your solution to find the failing case.

blocks.text: **Stress testing** finds elusive bugs: write a slow but obviously-correct **brute force**, a **random generator**, and a script that runs both until outputs differ — giving you a small failing case to debug.
When you're sure the logic is right but it's WA, stress test — it beats staring at code.

mcqs.q: Stress testing compares your solution against:
mcqs.explain: A trusted brute force reveals mismatches.
You get a minimal counterexample to debug.

mcqs.q: Stress testing is most useful when:
options: Logic seems right but it's WA
mcqs.explain: It surfaces hidden edge-case bugs.
